source: CARDI (2011), "Handbook of Integrated Techniques for Increasing Wet-Season and Dry-Season Rice Productivity" (Khmer, 50pp, funded by CAVAC/ACIAR, foreword by H.E. Chan Sarun, Minister of Agriculture, dated 26 August 2011)
text: For eating/milling grain (not seed): common farmer practice is to store paddy in a raised granary (chrong) under or beside the house, protected against rats, mice and poultry; rats alone are estimated to eat only a modest amount directly (roughly 1 kg per m² of stored grain per month) but contaminate far more with urine and droppings, and can introduce disease. A simple, low-cost rat-guard is to wrap a smooth metal (tin/galvanized sheet) collar around each granary support post — cut it round with no sharp edge (to avoid injuring children) and wrap it snugly around the post before the granary is loaded, without leaving a ladder or anything else propped against the granary that a rat could climb, and keep the area around the granary clear so rats have no easy approach; also keep the granary well sealed against rain/damp so stored grain does not reabsorb moisture. An 8-month storage trial comparing an open-weave sack/open granary against a sealed (airtight) granary found: opened storage lost about 0.12% grain moisture and 0.42% grain weight after 1 month, rising to about 0.96% moisture and 3.36% weight loss after 8 months; sealed storage lost less over the same periods — about 0.10% moisture and 0.23% weight after 1 month, rising to about 0.80% moisture and 1.84% weight after 8 months — i.e. sealed storage roughly halves the cumulative weight loss of open storage over 8 months. For seed specifically: harvest at 21-25% moisture as usual, sun-dry in a 2–3 cm layer, turning regularly, until the seed reaches 13–13.5% moisture, then let it cool fully before bagging. Two storage approaches are used: (a) open storage — seed kept in ordinary sacks stacked in a store room, which can preserve seed quality for up to about 8 months if the store is kept dry, rainproof and rodent-proof, with each seed lot's sacks stacked separately, labelled, and periodically inspected and cleaned, and the store fumigated and cleaned between seasons; (b) sealed/airtight storage — using purpose-built containers such as a silo, a 'vulcanic cube'/cocoon-type flexible storage bag, or (for small farmer-scale lots) a plastic drum, metal drum, or a tightly-tied woven sack with the neck sealed shut — can keep seed in usable condition for as long as several years for large commercial volumes. Airtight storage works by cutting the oxygen available inside the container by roughly 10-15%, which stops storage insects from developing or surviving inside, and also slows the seed's own respiration rate, so the seed loses less weight and keeps quality longer than open storage. A parallel seed-viability trial over 10 months found sealed storage held germination and grain-weight loss steadier over time than open storage, whose germination rate declined faster.
caveat: Likely overlaps with existing KB storage/postharvest content (a standing open item flags 'postharvest numeric duplicate-checks'); moisture-loss and weight-loss percentages are read from two related but distinct source tables/charts (an 8-month grain-storage comparison and a 10-month seed-viability trial) and are kept separate here to avoid conflating them.
